title: Application of large volume injection for sensitive LC-MS/MS analysis of seven artificial sweeteners in surface waters
author: Henschel, Hayen

steps.title: Configure HPLC system and column
steps.instruction: Install the Kaseisorb LC ODS‑SAX Super column (150 × 2.0 mm, 3.0 µm; TCI) on the Agilent 1100 series HPLC, set the column temperature to 40 °C and the mobile‑phase flow rate to 0.25 mL min⁻¹.

steps.title: Prepare mobile phases
steps.instruction: Make mobile‑phase A by dissolving ammonium formate to a final concentration of 20 mM and adjusting the pH to 3.5; mobile‑phase B is acetonitrile (ACN). Mix them to give an initial composition of 85 % A : 15 % B (v/v).

steps.title: Program gradient for mixed‑mode separation
steps.instruction: Set a two‑step gradient: start with 15 % ACN (mobile‑phase B) from 0 to 5 min, then increase to 40 % ACN, and finally to 80 % ACN as illustrated in Fig. 2. Maintain the initial 85 % A : 15 % B composition before the gradient begins.

steps.title: Load sample and set injection volume
steps.instruction: Connect the Agilent multidraw upgrade kit (400 µL extension) and the 100 µL sample loop to the HPLC. Begin with a 10 µL injection to verify system performance, then perform large‑volume injections (LVI) of 500 µL of the surface‑water sample, allowing refocusing at the column head.

steps.title: Configure mass spectrometer source
steps.instruction: Set the EVOQ Elite™ triple‑quadrupole (Bruker) to positive/negative switching mode, apply a heated electrospray voltage of ±4000 V, set cone and heated‑probe temperature to 350 °C, and adjust gas flows to: cone gas 20 units, probe gas 40 units, nebulizer gas 60 units.

steps.title: Run LC‑MS/MS analysis
steps.instruction: Start the LC gradient, inject the 500 µL sample, and acquire data using the programmed MRM transitions in positive/negative switching mode. Use Compass Hystar 4.0 and MS Workstation (Bruker) for instrument control, data acquisition, and evaluation.

description: Artificial sweeteners as sugar substitutes have become popular in today's calorie-conscious society. The significant increase in application results in the presence of some persistent compounds in the aquatic environment, detectable in the effluent of waste water plants and even in mineral water [1], [2], [3], [4]. The structural features of artificial sweeteners are highly diverse, and thus complicate the chromatographic separation of multiple compounds with a single technique [5]. Therefore, a method was developed using mixed-mode chromatography on a stationary phase with C18-akyl and anion exchange properties. The separation of (i) three anionic sulfamates (acesulfame, cyclamate, saccharin), (ii) two zwitterionic dipeptides (aspartame, neotame), and (iii) two polar derivates of the natural products sucralose and neohesperidin dihydrochalcone (NHDC) was achieved. Although the use of hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) columns has proven to be a successful approach for the analysis of polar sweeteners [6,7], the mixed-mode separation showed improved peak shapes and HILIC is not compatible with the direct injection of large volumes when the injection solvent is water, as investigated in detail by Ruta et al. [8]. The simultaneous investigation of these seven partly persistent artificial sweeteners in surface water requires a highly sensitive detection technique, commonly accompanied with a preconcentration strategy. Solid phase extractions (SPE) for analytes with a broad polarity range can be complex as well as costly and time-consuming [9]. Hence, the implementation of a large volume injection (LVI) represents a suitable alternative to extraction techniques. Furthermore, the developed mixed-mode method operated in reversed-phase mode allowing LVIs up to 500 µL. This increase in injected volume combined with a refocusing at the column head improved the limits of detection and quantification to the low and sub-ng L1 concentration range. Common LVI i
